heading_en: Positioning of Mono-ruby with Respect to Base Characters
heading_ja: モノルビの親文字に対する配置位置

cases.quote: When attaching a single hiragana (cl-15) ruby character to a single base character, there are two ways of positioning the ruby character.
cases.rationale: §3.3.5's own two enumerated methods, nakatsuki (中付き, center-alignment) and katatsuki (肩付き, top/left-alignment), are `jlreq_spec::Question::RUBY_ALIGNMENT`'s two choices, and `jlreq_inline::lower` genuinely reads the question now (M4-a round 1): absent a per-construct `Ruby::with_alignment` override — this case declares none, and `cases.schema.json`'s own `ruby` `$def` carries no field for one, deliberately (ADR-0019's per-construct-beats-policy precedence is this workspace's own bookkeeping, not something JLReq states, and is covered by unit tests in `crates/jlreq-inline/src/lower.rs` instead) — the resolved alignment is exactly the policy's own answer, `Contribution::alignment_of`'s own reading. `Policy::JLREQ` answers `nakatsuki`, JLReq's own default reading absent a stated preference, so the first entry is what `Kumihan::default()`'s own committed run genuinely measures; the second entry is genuinely measured too, as of this round (M4-a round 4): `crates/jlreq-conform/tests/suite.rs`'s own `section_3_3_5_is_also_measured_under_katatsuki` constructs a second `Kumihan::new(Policy)` declaring `ruby.alignment: katatsuki`, under which this entry — naming that one question — is the selected reading rather than `{}`, and the assertion is a real, checked agreement rather than a statement published for another implementation alone.

permitted.source: `Policy::JLREQ`'s own default answer to `ruby.alignment` (nakatsuki), the reading this workspace measures by default where §3.3.5 states two permitted methods
§3.3.5's own second method, katatsuki — a statement to an implementation that declares this alternative; this workspace's own default run does not select it

cases.quote: In vertical writing mode, attach a ruby character so that the top of its virtual body is aligned with the top of that of the base character (see Figure 119). This positioning of a ruby character is called 'katatsuki' (top-alignment). For horizontal writing mode, 'katatsuki' should not be adopted. If a ruby character is attached so that the left-edge of its virtual body is aligned with the left-edge of that of the base character, it would result in the loss of the center of balance, which doesn't look good (see Figure 120).
cases.rationale: The quoted sentence states a recommendation against katatsuki in horizontal writing, not a prohibition — it says 'should not be adopted', never 'shall not' or 'is not permitted' — and ADR-0011 reads every such JLReq recommendation as honored and reported rather than refused. `jlreq_inline::lower` resolves the alignment `Contribution::alignment_of` reports regardless of `direction`, and separately records whether the combination is the discouraged one through `Contribution::alignment_discouraged`, read here as `alignment_discouraged`. The first entry is the baseline `Kumihan::default()`'s own committed run measures: nakatsuki is never the discouraged combination, in either writing direction, so `alignment_discouraged` reads `false` under `Policy::JLREQ`. The second entry is the fact this case exists to publish — katatsuki, resolved in this case's own declared horizontal writing, is `alignment_discouraged: true` and *still* `alignment: "katatsuki"`, not silently substituted for the undiscouraged reading — and, as of this round (M4-a round 4), it is genuinely measured, not only stated: `crates/jlreq-conform/tests/suite.rs`'s own `section_3_3_5_is_also_measured_under_katatsuki` runs this file's own cases a second time against a `Kumihan::new(Policy)` declaring `ruby.alignment: katatsuki`, under which this entry is the selected reading and the discouraged-but-honored assertion is checked rather than merely published; `crates/jlreq-inline/src/lower.rs`'s own `katatsuki_is_honored_and_discouraged_only_in_horizontal_writing` unit test still exercises it directly too, against both writing directions.

permitted.source: `Policy::JLREQ`'s own default, nakatsuki — never the discouraged combination in either writing direction

the katatsuki reading, resolved in this case's own declared horizontal writing — discouraged by the quoted sentence but honored, never refused (ADR-0011) — a statement to an implementation that declares this alternative; this workspace's own default run does not select it

cases.quote: In vertical writing mode, attach a ruby character so that its vertical center matches that of the base character (see Figure 119). In horizontal writing mode, attach a ruby character so that its horizontal center matches that of the base character (see Figure 119). This positioning of a ruby character is called 'nakatsuki' (center-alignment). ... In vertical writing mode, attach a ruby character so that the top of its virtual body is aligned with the top of that of the base character (see Figure 119). This positioning of a ruby character is called 'katatsuki' (top-alignment). For horizontal writing mode, 'katatsuki' should not be adopted.
cases.rationale: §3.3.5(b)'s own load-bearing pair, reused from `3.3.5/ruby-alignment/policy-selects-nakatsuki-or-katatsuki`'s own input with `kind` changed to `place`: the same run, positioned two ways. One base item, so there is no interior boundary for this case to ask about at all and no Table 1 coordinate to verify blank — the question is vacuous rather than needing a citation. `jlreq::place`'s own derivation (`Compose::place`'s own doc in `crates/jlreq-conform/src/kumihan.rs`) puts the base at `placements[0] = 0`, the sum of nothing before it. Nakatsuki centers: the base's own supplied advance (1000) and the run's own summed advance (500) differ by 500, `distribute` splits it evenly into two 250-unit shares under `Policy::JLREQ`'s own leading-remainder default (the split is exact here, so the remainder rule never has to break a tie), and the leading share shifts the run's own start from the base placement — 0 + 250 = 250. Katatsuki start-aligns: §3.3.5(b) states the katatsuki method unconditionally for a single ruby character — align the start edge of the ruby's own virtual body with the start edge of the base's, quoted above as the top-to-top alignment of vertical writing and rendered left-to-left in horizontal, one inline-axis fact stated twice in physical axes. No comparison between the run's and the base's own lengths is stated for the one-character case; that comparison first appears in §3.3.5(c), for three-or-more ruby characters. The run therefore starts exactly at the base's own placement, 0. `crates/jlreq-inline/src/place.rs`'s own `nakatsuki_and_katatsuki_place_a_one_character_run_at_different_offsets` unit test independently derives and pins the identical two offsets over the identical fixture; this case's own arithmetic above was worked from §3.3.5(b)'s own words and §5's own arithmetic rather than read out of either.

permitted.source: `Policy::JLREQ`'s own default answer to `ruby.alignment` (nakatsuki), centered under §3.3.5(b)'s first method
§3.3.5(b)'s second method, katatsuki, start-aligned with no distribution

cases.quote: When attaching two hiragana (cl-15) ruby characters to a single base character, the lengths of the ruby text and the base text are the same and they are positioned as shown in Figure 118.
cases.rationale: §3.3.5(a)'s own equal-length case, and the point of publishing only one `permitted` entry is itself the assertion: at this exact ratio the two alignment methods §3.3.5(b) states are not two readings but one. One base item (鬼, 1000 units), so `placements[0] = 0` and there is no interior boundary to verify blank. Nakatsuki: the base (1000) and the run's own summed advance (500 + 500 = 1000) are equal, so the centering difference is zero, `distribute` splits zero into two zero shares, and the run starts exactly at the base placement, 0. Katatsuki: §3.3.5(b) defines katatsuki as aligning the left edge of the ruby's own virtual body with the left edge of the base's virtual body (in horizontal writing), so the run starts exactly where the base starts, 0, independent of any length comparison between run and base — nakatsuki's own centering, worked above, reaches that same 0 here only because base and run happen to be equal-length, so the two methods agree at this one ratio rather than by shared machinery. Both methods therefore place the first ruby character at 0; `place_solid_run` then lays the second out solid, at the first's own 500-unit advance past it, regardless of which alignment resolved — 500. A second `permitted` entry naming `ruby.alignment: katatsuki` would repeat these identical two numbers under a different policy key, which would not assert a second reading, only restate the first under a label that invites a reader to expect one; `crates/jlreq-inline/src/place.rs`'s own `two_ruby_characters_exactly_filling_the_base_agree_under_both_alignments` unit test demonstrates the identical agreement falling out rather than being special-cased, over the identical fixture, and this case's own arithmetic was worked independently from §3.3.5(a)'s and (b)'s own words rather than read out of it.

permitted.source: §3.3.5(a)'s own equal-length case, alignment-independent by construction — see this case's own rationale for why a second, katatsuki-naming entry would not be a second reading

cases.quote: When attaching three or more hiragana (cl-15) ruby characters to a single base character, the ruby characters are set solid. In this case, where the length of a ruby text is longer than that of its base character, positioning of the ruby text depends on which alignment has been adopted for a single ruby character. ... When nakatsuki alignment is adopted for a single ruby character, position a ruby text so that its vertical center is aligned with that of its base character in vertical writing mode (see Figure 121). In horizontal writing mode, position a ruby text so that its horizontal center is aligned with that of its base character (see Figure 121). ... When katatsuki alignment is adopted for a single ruby character, there are two methods, as follows: (i) Position the ruby text so that its vertical center is aligned with that of its base character (see Figure 121). (ii) Depending on the type of script of the adjacent characters to the base character, and the number of ruby characters, a decision is made about whether ruby hangover is allowed on the character before its base character, or on the character after, or on both adjacent characters. At break-even situation, the hangover is usually on the character after its base character (see Figure 122).
cases.rationale: §3.3.5(c) in full, over a base of two items so the nakatsuki reading is a realistic offset rather than a negative one starting before the paragraph: item 0 (あ, hiragana, cl-15) at 1000 units, item 1 (鬼, ideographic, cl-19) at 1000 units carrying a three-character reading (かかか) of 600 units each, 1800 total — 800 units longer than its own base. The coordinate is chosen deliberately: cl-15 against cl-19 is `blank` in Table 1 (`spec/captured/table1.en.tsv`, line 427, read directly rather than inferred from this evaluator's own answer), so the derived solid layout §3 of this round's own brief requires (`Compose::place`'s own doc) is faithful at this boundary — nothing conditional is omitted by treating it as solid. The neighbor is chosen deliberately too, and not merely for the blank cell: §3.3.8 rule 1 forces a mono-ruby base apart from an adjacent character only when that neighbor resolves to cl-19, exactly what `3.3.8/forced-separation/only-beside-ideographic-neighbors` already establishes in both directions over a hiragana neighbor (no separation) and an ideographic one (a forced separation) — item 0 here is hiragana, cl-15, so `collect_mono_separation`'s own left-neighbor check never fires, no forced separation arises at the boundary before item 1, and `derived_placements` never has to add one. This is checked, not assumed: with no separation, `placements[0] = 0` and `placements[1] = 1000`, the sum of item 0's own advance and nothing else — the identical number a real forced separation would have changed, so the absence is load-bearing to the case's own arithmetic and not merely convenient. Nakatsuki centers unconditionally: the base (1000) and the run (1800) differ by 1000 − 1800 = −800, `distribute` splits it into two −400 shares, and the run starts at `placements[1] + (−400) = 600`; `place_solid_run` then lays the three ruby characters out solid at their own 600-unit advances — 600, 1200, 1800. §3.3.5(c) states only the centering method for nakatsuki, with no alternative, so `declined` is empty. Katatsuki declines: the run (1800) is longer than the base (1000) — exactly the condition §3.3.5(c) itself opens its katatsuki paragraph with, 'where the length of a ruby text is longer than that of its base character' — and for exactly this case §3.3.5(c) states two named methods under katatsuki: center after all, or decide which neighbor the hangover falls on by script and character count — naming no preference between them; `spec/derived/questions.tsv`'s own §3.3.5 neighborhood carries `ruby.alignment`, `ruby.group_distribution`, `ruby.jukugo_layout`, `ruby.overhang_kana` and `ruby.overhang_indent`, and none of the five is this choice, so `place()` declines on its own authority rather than picking (task #81 is where that choice gets a `Question`). `declined` names the specific construct ordinal, 0 — the only declared `constructs.ruby` entry — rather than merely being non-empty, because 'nothing was placed' is satisfiable by an implementation that never placed anything at all; naming the ordinal is satisfiable only by one that reached this branch and declined there.

permitted.source: `Policy::JLREQ`'s own default answer to `ruby.alignment` (nakatsuki), centered under §3.3.5(c)'s own first bullet — the only method the section states for it

§3.3.5(c)'s own katatsuki-with-overflow choice, stated as two methods with no preference between them and no policy `Question` yet to select one (task #81); `place()` declines rather than picking on its own authority
